title: 133 Days Alone on a Raft. He Made a Fish Hook From a Flashlight #shorts
description:
Case 009. On 23 November 1942 the British cargo steamer SS Benlomond, sailing alone from Cape Town toward Paramaribo, was hit by two torpedoes from the German submarine U-172 in the Atlantic, roughly 750 miles east of the Amazon. She sank in about two minutes. Poon Lim, a 24-year-old second steward from Hainan, China, went over the side in a life jacket and, after about two hours in the water, found an empty wooden life raft about eight feet square. It carried biscuits, water and a few other stores. When they ran low he made a fish hook from the spring of the raft's flashlight and a bigger one from a nail, used rope as line, cut his catch with a knife made from a tin, caught rain in canvas, and took seabirds and even a shark. A freighter passed without stopping and patrol planes that had spotted him lost him in a storm. On 5 April 1943, after 133 days, three Brazilian fishermen picked him up off the coast of Pará; he had lost about 20 pounds. He was the only survivor of more than 50 men aboard. He received the British Empire Medal, later became a US citizen and died in Brooklyn in 1991. Guinness World Records still lists his 133 days as the longest survival alone on a raft. Rook didn't believe it either.

Animated reconstruction of a true story.

source_notes: Read for this run (fetched 14 Nov 2026): Guinness World Records ('Longest time adrift at sea - alone'), uboat.net (ship page for Benlomond), Wikipedia (Poon Lim; SS Benlomond (1922)), War History Online and Today I Found Out. The strong sources are Guinness, uboat.net and the US Navy caption to photo 80-G-42356 (July 1943, read second-hand via Wikipedia); the popular articles largely repeat Wikipedia, which cites the New York Times of 17 July 1943 and London Gazette 36091, neither of which this run could open. Agreed: SS Benlomond of the Ben Line, unescorted, between Cape Town and Paramaribo; sunk 23 November 1942 by U-172 with two torpedoes; sank in about two minutes (uboat.net, both Wikipedia pages); Poon Lim was the second (mess) steward and the only survivor (Guinness, uboat.net, Wikipedia); born in Hainan in March 1918, so 24 at the sinking (Wikipedia, the popular articles; the US Navy caption calls him 25 in July 1943, which fits); about two hours in the water before he found the raft; a wooden raft about eight feet square with biscuits/hardtack, water and other stores, flares and a flashlight; a fish hook made from the flashlight's spring (US Navy caption and every other source), a larger hook from a nail, hemp rope as line, rain caught in canvas, seabirds and a shark caught; a passing freighter that did not pick him up and US Navy patrol planes that saw him before a storm moved him; rescue on 5 April 1943 by three Brazilian fishermen about ten miles off the coast of Para, landed at Belem three days later; about 20 lb / 9 kg lost; British Empire Medal; US citizenship in 1952; died in Brooklyn on 4 January 1991; Guinness: 'the longest recorded survival alone on a raft is 133 days', still listed. Where the sources differ: (1) Men aboard: 54 with 53 lost (uboat.net) or 53 with 52 lost (Wikipedia); the description says 'more than 50' and the film gives no number. (2) Position: 0.5 N 38.75 W (uboat.net, ship article) or 0.3 N 38.45 W (Poon Lim article); the sketch map uses the first and is labelled a sketch. (3) Birthplace: Hainan (Wikipedia and others) or 'Hong Kong-born' (Guinness); the crew-file insert says Hainan, China. (4) How long the stores lasted: food about 55 days and water about 70 (Wikipedia, US Navy caption) or rationed for 30 days (Today I Found Out); the script says only 'Then nothing' and gives no figure. (5) The knife: cut from a biscuit tin (War History Online) or a pemmican tin (Wikipedia); the script says 'a tin'. (6) Rescue date 5 April (Guinness, uboat.net, Wikipedia) or 4 April (US Navy caption); the map says 5 April. (7) Some sources count 132 days; Guinness says 133. (8) Whether he walked ashore unaided (Guinness) or had to be lifted off the raft (Wikipedia); not shown or stated. (9) Hospital stay of four weeks or two; not stated. (10) Other men were seen on a second raft that drifted away and was never found (Wikipedia), and uboat.net says the U-boat's crew questioned survivors; nobody else was ever rescued, the film does not show this. Left out on purpose: his belief that the freighter did not stop because he was Chinese / might be taken for Japanese (reported as his view by Wikipedia and others; a Short has no room to present it fairly, so the film says only that the ship did not stop; the label reads IT KEEPS GOING); drinking the shark's blood; the quote often attributed to him about hoping nobody breaks the record (wording varies and no primary source was found, so it is not used). No dialogue is attributed to anyone. Shown but not narrated, from the sources: the life jacket, the U-boat and the torpedo track, the knotted rope for counting days (Wikipedia, The Vintage News), fish strips drying on a line (Wikipedia), the canvas awning (Wikipedia, Today I Found Out), 23 NOV 1942 and 5 APR 1943 on the map. Dramatised, not reported: the look of the ship (a generic grey 1920s steamer with no name, flag or company colours), of the submarine (no number or emblem), of the passing freighter and the patrol plane (generic twin-engined flying boat, no markings); the raft's floats, poles and exact layout, the tins' colours and the water can; how he looked and dressed; the gull landing on Rook's hat and the way the bird is caught; the shark circling at the surface (sources say he hooked a small shark, not how it approached); the storm's lightning; the fishermen's boat, sail, hats and clothes and their number in the last shot; the hand clasp; the coastline; the crew-file card (a drawn silhouette, not a photograph; no such document is claimed); the dotted drift line (its real path is unknown and the map says so); the harbour pier; and everything Rook does. Rook is never the one in danger in the sad beats: he drops the jokes when the freighter passes.

quality_gate.method: 3D contact sheet reviewed in four rounds with fixes after each (round 1: night scenes were too dark, the swimmer, the climb onto the raft, the supplies, the spring-to-hook close-up, the tin knife, the hand clasp and the last boat shot were unreadable and were restaged, two shots had the awning or the frame edge cutting heads; round 2: moonlight on the steamer and the submarine, shark kept inside the tall frame, hook close-up restacked vertically, boat cast regrouped; round 3: the hook was rebuilt as a real hook shape instead of a ring, the gull folds its wings when it lands, the submarine shot was re-lit and re-framed; round 4: three fishermen visible, Rook's face readable in the rain, map labels separated), then a full-length low-resolution rehearsal (216x384, 4 samples, every 3D frame) composited with captions, HUD, overlays, inserts and sound, reviewed on a composite contact sheet and frame strips of nine shots, plus four shots at production quality. The rehearsal passed the automated gate locally: 37 shots, mean 1.28 s, longest 1.84 s, loudness -15.0 LUFS, voice 11.8 dB over the bed, host in 18/37 shots (49%), closest match to an earlier episode 0.75. Caption pairs were measured against the frame width and three lines were reworded where a pair was too wide. Audio was measured, not listened to. The full-resolution render and the final gate run in the cloud.
